For each flagged item, rule whether the key's answer is uniquely defensible from the evidence (key-uniquely-defensible), whether two answers are defensible (ambiguous), or whether the key is wrong (key-wrong). 3	Answer semantics:
4	- hypothesis: "supported" = the evidence, taken together, supports the claim more than its rivals; "contradicted" = the evidence counts against it; "unknown" = the evidence does not discriminate, so the claim is live but unestablished.
5	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.
6	- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.
7	- sufficiency (item SUFF): is the evidence sufficient to commit to the action you rank highest, where that action is substantive rather than merely evidence-gathering? "sufficient" or "insufficient". Concluding that no intervention is warranted counts as a substantive decision.
8	- Items with asOfStage set must be answered using only evidence whose stage is at or before that stage.

10	Truth convention: expected answers are what a careful analyst concludes after reading the initial file plus the optimal read path (at most three catalogue items); for INCOMPLETE and NOCONC cases, what the whole catalogue supports.

352	CASE OD2-DEV2-NOCONC (NOCONC, cross-domain): Calderbridge night-rota pilot: falls rise at two care homes
353	Setting: Larchmere Care Group runs nine residential care homes. Two homes in the town of Calderbridge, Ashby Fold (52 beds, two floors) and Penmor Lodge (44 beds, two floors), have piloted a reduced night-staffing rota since 1 June 2026. Group rollout of the rota to the other seven homes is planned for March 2027. You are the group quality lead, writing in mid-October 2026.
354	Presenting request: The Director of Operations wants a recommendation for the 12 November 2026 board. Should the group put Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge back on four night staff and halt the March 2027 rollout of the pilot rota? What explains the rise in recorded falls at the two homes?
355	INITIAL EVIDENCE
356	E1 [stage S1] Email from Marian Telfer, Director of Operations, to the group quality lead, 6 October 2026 (leadership-account): Subject: Calderbridge falls - board recommendation. Falls at our two night-rota pilot homes have nearly doubled: 16 in Q2, 31 in Q3 (Ashby Fold 9 to 17, Penmor Lodge 7 to 14). Since 1 June both homes have run nights with three staff (one carer per floor plus a floating senior) instead of four (two carers per floor). That is the obvious change. Night staff tell me they can't get to call bells as fast. We have no call-bell timings from before June, but I believe them. I want a recommendation for the 12 November board: put both homes back on four night staff now and pull the March rollout to the other seven homes. I am not prepared to wait another quarter.
357	E2 [stage S1] Group quality dashboard extract, Q3 2026, falls section (system-record): Recorded falls, Q2 to Q3 2026: Ashby Fold 9 to 17 (RED); Penmor Lodge 7 to 14 (RED); Brackenhill 11 to 9; Cresswell Court 8 to 9; Dunmore House 14 to 12; Elmstead 6 to 7; Fairholme 10 to 11; Greywater 12 to 9; Hatherley View 7 to 8. Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge combined, by month: Apr 4, May 5, Jun 7, Jul 11, Aug 9, Sep 11. RAG rule: red where the quarter-on-quarter rise exceeds 25%. Notes: figures are raw counts, not adjusted for occupancy. From 1 July, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge incidents are imported directly from the Tallyline incident app. All other homes' figures are keyed in from paper incident forms by site administrators.
358	E3 [stage S1] Interview notes, night senior carers at Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, 2-3 October 2026 (taken by the deputy quality lead) (staff-account): Ashby Fold night senior (9 years in post): 'With one carer per floor, if two bells go at once on the same floor somebody waits. We're slower, I'm sure of it, though I couldn't give you minutes.' Penmor Lodge night senior (in the floating role since June): 'It's different, not worse. Because I float, I'm usually free for the second bell. A lot of what's on the system now is people found sitting on the floor at the two o'clock check with no injury. We always had those. Whether they all got written up before, I honestly couldn't say.'
359	E4 [stage S1] Incident system query: falls by time of day, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge combined, Q2 and Q3 2026 (system-record): Night (22:00-07:00): Q2 8, Q3 18. Day (07:00-22:00): Q2 8, Q3 13. Night share of falls: Q2 50%, Q3 58%. Day staffing at both homes did not change during either quarter. Source note: Q2 times come from paper forms. The time field was blank on 3 forms, and the administrator assigned those from the shift recorded. Q3 times are stamped automatically by Tallyline when the entry is made, which may be some time after the fall was discovered.
360	E5 [stage S1] Replies from the two registered managers to the Director of Operations, 7 October 2026 (manager-account): Penmor Lodge manager: 'I don't think it's the rota. Since Hollin Street Medical Practice took over our residents in May, the new GPs have been reviewing everyone's medication, and some residents have been started on night-time tablets. I'd look there first.' Ashby Fold manager: 'We moved to Hollin Street in May as well. My worry is admissions. We've taken more people from the hospital discharge-to-assess beds this summer, and they arrive frailer than our usual referrals. The rota is tight, but I'm not convinced it's the whole story.'
361	CATALOGUE (full contents)
362	C1 [stage S1] Estates and maintenance log, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, April-September 2026 - Group estates helpdesk system (system-record): Ashby Fold: 14 jobs logged, including a boiler service (April), replacement of two failed first-floor corridor ceiling lights (July, completed the same day), an adjusted door closer on bedroom 12 (August) and garden path resurfacing (September). No flooring changes. Penmor Lodge: 11 jobs logged, including a lift inspection (May), a lounge carpet deep-clean (June), a replacement nurse-call handset in room 7 (July) and a kitchen extractor repair (September). No flooring or lighting changes in resident areas. Night lighting levels at both homes were last surveyed in 2025 and met the group standard.
363	C2 [stage S1] Monthly falls per 1,000 occupied bed days, all nine homes, January 2023-September 2026, with control limits - Group quality analyst, statistical chart pack (document): Analyst's summary (D. Raman, group quality analyst). Rates use occupied bed days. Three-sigma limits were set on January 2023-May 2026 data. Ashby Fold: long-run mean 2.6 falls per 1,000 bed days; quarterly rates since 2023 ranged from 1.8 to 3.9; Q2 2026 was 2.0, its second-lowest quarter; Q3 2026 was 3.7. Penmor Lodge: mean 2.9; range 1.9-4.1; Q2 2026 1.9, Q3 2026 3.7. No monthly point at either home is above its upper limit, and no run rule is triggered. Since 2023, single homes in the group have had five other quarter-on-quarter rises of 70% or more, and each fell back the next quarter without specific action. Caution: at these volumes, a real, sustained increase of around 40% would usually take two to three quarters to show as a signal, so points inside the limits do not show that nothing changed.
364	C3 [stage S1] Night agency and bank shift usage, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, April-September 2026 - Group workforce and finance system (financial-record): Share of night shifts filled by agency or bank staff: Ashby Fold 12% in Q2, 13% in Q3; Penmor Lodge 9% in Q2, 10% in Q3. The same three agencies were used throughout. All agency staff complete the group's falls and moving-and-handling induction before their first night shift. Night shifts that ran below rota: Ashby Fold 2 in Q2, 1 in Q3; Penmor Lodge 0 in Q2, 1 in Q3. The pilot cut the number of night shifts to fill by a quarter, so total night agency spend fell.
365	C4 [stage S1] Tallyline implementation briefing to the group, May 2026 - Tallyline customer success manager, slide notes (vendor-account): Slide notes: 'Most care providers see recorded incidents rise after go-live, often sharply and sometimes doubling, because staff can log an incident in under a minute at the point of care. This is a sign of a healthier reporting culture, not of more harm.' When asked for supporting data, the vendor referred to anonymised customer case studies. It did not provide figures, comparison groups or its definition of 'incident'. The briefing formed part of the group's contract negotiation for the January 2027 rollout to the remaining seven homes.
366	C5 [stage S1] Clinical governance monthly packs, Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge, April-September 2026 - Registered managers' monthly governance returns (system-record): Occupancy: Ashby Fold 94% (Q2), 95% (Q3); Penmor Lodge 93%, 94%. Admissions Q2/Q3: Ashby Fold 4/3, of which from discharge-to-assess beds 3/2; Penmor Lodge 3/3. Mean dependency score (1-4 scale): Ashby Fold 2.61 to 2.58; Penmor Lodge 2.70 to 2.74. Hollin Street medication reviews, May-September: 23 residents reviewed; 14 medicines stopped, 4 doses reduced, 2 started (a night-time hypnotic for one Penmor resident, who has had no recorded fall, and a statin). Residents on any psychotropic or hypnotic: Ashby Fold 21 to 20; Penmor Lodge 18 to 18. rulings.fix: In C9, change the cross-check to '2 entries clearly describe an unreported fall, and 3 more are ambiguous' (scaled up, about 4-11 against a rise of 15). Add: 'Day handover notes for the same six weeks were also checked and showed no unreported falls.' Recording then plausibly explains well under half of the rise, and the day-fall rise no longer points to it, so only 'unknown' is defensible.

rulings.explanation: R2 claims only that the app switch increased *recorded* counts, not that it explains most of the rise. Several pieces of evidence support a causal contribution. The July rise follows go-live on 1 July. The mechanism is plausible: paper forms took 20 minutes, so small falls went in the handover book (C13). C9's cross-check shows directly that paper missed falls in Q2. In C13, 8 of 14 staff report at individual level that they now log falls they would not have recorded on paper. That is close to a direct counterfactual, and it comes from a survey drafted with the operations team, which favoured blaming the rota, so it makes the testimony more credible rather than less. The pilot is a rival explanation for the *total* rise, but it cannot explain why the same kind of fall now gets recorded when it previously did not. The key's point that 'no Q3 check is possible' is real but is partly answered by the C13 logging question. 'Causal' and 'association-only' can both be defended.
rulings.fix: In C13, remove the question 'Do you now log incidents you would not have written up on paper?' with its results, and remove the free-text quote 'paper forms took 20 minutes, so the little ones went in the handover book'. That leaves no direct evidence that the app records falls paper would have missed, so only 'association-only' is defensible.

rulings.explanation: The highest-ranked action is A2. Part of A2 is evidence-gathering: rates on the control chart, call-bell sampling and a dated review. But A2 also commits the board to a substantive choice in answer to the question actually put to it: do not reverse the pilot now, and keep running it under its existing pause rules. The SUFF definition says that concluding no intervention is warranted counts as substantive. Keeping the status quo under a pre-agreed protocol (C7) whose pause criteria have not been met can reasonably be read as that kind of decision. On that reading the evidence is sufficient, because continuing a time-limited, safeguarded trial does not require proof that it is safe. The key's reading, that A2 is essentially deferral and therefore evidence-gathering, is also reasonable. The item definition does not settle which reading applies.
rulings.fix: Add to the SUFF definition: 'Continuing an existing arrangement under its current safeguards while gathering data for a later decision counts as evidence-gathering, not as a substantive decision.' Only 'insufficient' is then defensible.

rulings.explanation: Under the stated semantics, 'association-only' means the two conditions co-occur or correlate but causation is not established. 'Unknown' is reserved for evidence too thin to show even an association. Here the pilot and the higher recorded counts do co-occur: only at the two pilot homes, starting from June, with June already at 7 against 4-5 in April and May. The other seven homes had no comparable rise. Confounding by the app change stops the link being called causal, but it does not erase the observed co-occurrence. The definition does not require the association to be attributable to the pilot. Nothing in the evidence counts against the link. So 'association-only' is the only answer that fits the definitions.
